title: Lists
subtitle: ul, ol, li, dl — organise your content

whyItExists.short: Lists are one of the most common content patterns on the web. HTML has dedicated elements for unordered lists, ordered lists, and description lists.
whyItExists.problem: Manually writing '1. 2. 3.' in text means browsers, screen readers, and search engines have no idea that content is a list.
whyItExists.solution: ul/ol/li create real list semantics — screen readers announce 'list of 5 items', search engines understand list structure, and CSS can style bullets freely.
whyItExists.impact: Navigation menus, step-by-step guides, feature lists, and FAQs are all built with HTML lists.

explainModes.beginner: ul is a bullet list (unordered). ol is a numbered list (ordered). li is each item inside either. dl is for term-definition pairs, like a glossary.
explainModes.simple: HTML has three list types: ul (bullets), ol (numbers), and dl (description/glossary). Items go inside li for ul/ol, or inside dt/dd pairs for dl.
explainModes.standard: ul and ol both contain li elements. The difference is semantic — ul is for items with no meaningful order; ol is for sequences where order matters. dl pairs a term (dt) with one or more definitions (dd). All three types can be nested.
explainModes.technical: ul/ol have implicit ARIA role `list`; li has role `listitem`. dl maps to role `definition`, dt to `term`, dd to `definition`. Nesting lists beyond 2–3 levels hurts readability and screen-reader announcements. CSS list-style-type can replace or remove bullets/numbers entirely.
explainModes.deepDive: Navigation menus are almost always ul > li > a structures — the semantic list conveys that the links form a related group. Screen readers announce 'navigation, list of 5 items' and allow users to skip the list. ol's start, reversed, and type attributes allow custom counters. The value attribute on individual li elements sets an explicit counter value.

content.text: HTML has three list elements, each for a different purpose:

items: **ul** (unordered list) — bullets, for items with no required order
**ol** (ordered list) — numbers, for steps or ranked items
**dl** (description list) — term/definition pairs, for glossaries or metadata

content.title: ol start attribute
content.body: Use start="5" on ol to begin numbering at 5, useful for continuing a list broken by other content.

content.label: Description list — glossary
content.code:
<dl>
  <dt>HTML</dt>
  <dd>HyperText Markup Language — the structure of web pages</dd>

  <dt>CSS</dt>
  <dd>Cascading Style Sheets — the visual presentation of web pages</dd>

  <dt>JavaScript</dt>
  <dd>A programming language that makes web pages interactive</dd>
</dl>

content.text: Lists can be **nested** — place a new ul or ol inside an li to create sub-lists.

content.question: Which list type should you use for a step-by-step installation guide?
content.explanation: ol (ordered list) is correct because the order of the steps matters. ul is for unordered items; dl is for term-definition pairs.

content.question: Which element goes directly inside ul or ol?
content.explanation: Only li elements are valid direct children of ul and ol. dt and dd are used inside dl only.

faq.q: Can I put a p inside an li?
faq.a: Yes. li can contain block-level content including p, blockquote, and even nested lists. This is common for complex list items.

faq.q: How do I remove the default bullets with CSS?
faq.a: Use list-style: none on the ul or ol. Also add padding: 0 and margin: 0 since browsers add default spacing.

faq.q: When should I use dl vs a table?
faq.a: Use dl for pairs of terms and their descriptions (glossaries, metadata). Use a table when you have multiple properties per item across rows and columns.

examples: Every navigation bar on the web is a ul > li > a pattern
MDN's sidebar is a nested ul with hundreds of li items
